rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$PV=nRT,\qquad PV=\frac{m}{M}RT,\qquad PM=dRT,\qquad P=CRT$$
$$R=8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}=0.0821\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}=2\ \text{cal K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$$
$$k=\frac{R}{N_{A}}=1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1},\quad KE_{\text{molar}}=\frac{3}{2}RT,\quad C_{p}-C_{v}=R$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ An ideal gas is merely a light gas such as hydrogen. ✅ Ideality is about behaviour (no forces, no molecular volume), not mass; hydrogen merely approaches it best.  ·  ❌ R changes from gas to gas. ✅ R is universal; only the real-gas constants a and b differ between gases.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: 1 mol of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP (273 K, 1 atm) and 22.7 L at 273 K, 1 bar.  ·  R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 0.0821 L atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 1.987 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Molar mass of a gas with d = 1.25 g L⁻¹ at 27 °C and 1 atm. **Solution:** M = dRT/P = (1.25 × 0.0821 × 300)/1 ≈ 30.8 g mol⁻¹.  ·  **Problem:** Volume of 8 g O₂ at 27 °C and 750 mm Hg. **Solution:** n = 0.25 mol; V = nRT/P = (0.25 × 0.0821 × 300)/(750/760) ≈ 6.24 L.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: ideal gas, ideal gas equation, universal gas constant, its significance (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of an ideal gas  ·  An ideal (perfect) gas is a hypothetical gas that obeys the gas laws and PV = nRT exactly under all conditions. Its molecules are point masses with no volume and no intermolecular forces, and collisions are perfectly elastic. No real gas is ideal, but every gas approaches ideal behaviour at **low pressure and high temperature**.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Cp − Cv = R shows the molar heat capacity at constant pressure always exceeds that at constant volume.  ·  Ideal gas equation PV = nRT; from kinetic theory P = ⅓ (Nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so PV = ⅓N m⟨c²⟩.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. The ideal gas equation  ·  From Boyle (V ∝ 1/P), Charles (V ∝ T) and Avogadro (V ∝ n): $V\propto\frac{nT}{P}$, hence $PV=nRT$. Useful forms: $PV=\frac{m}{M}RT$ (mass m, molar mass M), $PM=dRT$ (density d) and $P=CRT$ for molar concentration C.  ·  ### 3. Meaning and value of R (universal gas constant)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: PV = nRT  ·  c_rms = √(3RT/M)  ·  KE_mole = 3RT/2

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ R and k are the same constant. ✅ k = R/N_A is the per-molecule (Boltzmann) constant.  ·  ❌ PV = nRT works at 100 atm without error. ✅ Deviation becomes severe (Z ≠ 1) and the van der Waals equation is required.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ ideal gas equation pv = nrt; from kinetic theory p = ⅓ (nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so pv = ⅓n m⟨c²⟩..

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Quote R's physical significance (work per mole per kelvin), not only its numerical value.  ·  Explain why R is called universal and give its value in three sets of units.  ·  Calculate the molar mass of a gas of density 1.25 g L⁻¹ at 27 °C and 1 atm.

rows.text: Find the volume occupied by 8 g of oxygen at 27 °C and 750 mm Hg.  ·  Discuss the significance of R in the kinetic theory and in thermodynamics.  ·  State the limitations of the ideal gas equation.
